claim: The human brain has the ability to derive knowledge from language inputs, in addition to nonlinguistic sensory channels such as vision and touch.
source: One signature of the human brain is its ability to derive knowledge from language inputs, in addition to nonlinguistic sensory channels such as vision and touch.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that frames the research question.

claim: Early deaf adults born to hearing parents had reduced early exposure and delayed acquisition of any natural human language (speech or sign).
source: early deaf adults who were born to hearing parents and had reduced early exposure and delayed acquisition of any natural human language (speech or sign)
evidence: This describes the participant characteristics of the delayed signer group.

claim: The deaf group with reduced early language exposure showed reduced semantic sensitivity in the left dorsal anterior temporal lobe (dATL) compared with the deaf control group.
source: The deaf group with reduced early language exposure, compared with the deaf control group, showed reduced semantic sensitivity, in both multivariate pattern (semantic structure encoding) and univariate (abstractness effect) analyses, in the left dorsal anterior temporal lobe (dATL).
evidence: This is the main finding reported in the abstract, supported by fMRI data analyses.

claim: Language experience drives the neural semantic representation in the dATL.
source: These results provide positive, causal evidence that language experience drives the neural semantic representation in the dATL, highlighting the roles of language in forming human neural semantic structures beyond nonverbal sensory experiences.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Modern neurocognitive theories of semantics share the view that semantic knowledge is ultimately grounded in nonlinguistic sensory/motor experiences.
source: A common view shared by the modern neurocognitive theories of semantics is that semantic knowledge, even those acquired through language, is ultimately grounded in (nonlinguistic) sensory/motor experiences, encoded in the distributed brain areas encompassing high-level sensorimotor areas, and potential hub regions that bind such sensory-derived representations (Barsalou, 2016; Binder et al., 2009; Fernandino et al., 2022; Ralph et al., 2017; Martin, 2016).
evidence: This statement summarizes existing theoretical frameworks with multiple citations.

claim: Language experiences may contribute to semantic development beyond sensory experiences by facilitating or modulating categorizations through labeling.
source: However, language experiences may contribute to semantic development beyond sensory experiences by facilitating or modulating categorizations by the nature of labeling (i.e. words) to the sensory experiences, and/or by constructing semantic relations based on various types of word relations (Gelman and Roberts, 2017; Perszyk and Waxman, 2018; Unger and Fisher, 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Congenitally blind individuals can acquire semantic structures about visual-specific knowledge (e.g., color) behaviorally similar to those in the sighted, presumably derived from language.
source: Congenitally blind individuals, who cannot acquire visual-specific knowledge (e.g. color) through sensory experiences, can nevertheless acquire semantic structures about such knowledge behaviorally similar to those in the sighted, presumably derived from language.
evidence: This statement describes findings from previous studies on blind individuals.

claim: Nonsensory semantic structures in the blind and sighted are represented in the dorsal anterior temporal lobe (dATL).
source: Such nonsensory semantic structures in the blind (and also sighted) are represented in the dorsal anterior temporal lobe (dATL), with sighted individuals additionally representing the highly similar knowledge structure (presumably derived from sensory experience) in the visual cortex (Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The dATL cluster is distinct from the central 'amodal' semantic hub located in the more ventral-medial territory of the ATL.
source: This dATL cluster is distinct from the central 'amodal' semantic hub proposed to bind together multiple sensory attributes, which is located in the more ventral-medial territory of the ATL (Ralph et al., 2017; Patterson et al., 2007; see discussions in Striem-Amit et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement distinguishes the dATL from other semantic regions based on cited literature.

claim: The left dATL is more strongly activated by abstract than concrete words in typically developed individuals.
source: The left dATL is also more strongly activated by abstract than concrete words in typically developed individuals (Binder et al., 2009; Bucur and Papagno, 2021; Wang et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: The dATL represents knowledge derived from language, in addition to those from sensory experiences in various perceptual regions.
source: It was thus proposed that this area represents knowledge derived from language, in addition to those from sensory experiences in various perceptual (association) regions (Bi, 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citation.

claim: Individuals who were born profoundly deaf in hearing families had limited natural language exposure (speech or sign) during early childhood.
source: Here, we address this issue in a special human model that varies in early language exposure: individuals who were born profoundly deaf in hearing families and had limited natural language exposure (speech or sign) during early childhood (Goldin-Meadow and Feldman, 1977; Mayberry et al., 2002).
evidence: This describes the participant model used in the study, supported by citations.

claim: Delayed deaf signers acquired their first language (sign language) around school age, which is much later than the age of first language acquisition in typically developed children or native deaf signers.
source: These individuals often acquired their first language (sign language) around school age, which is much later than the age of first language (L1) acquisition in typically developed children or in native deaf signers who were born in deaf families and acquired sign language from birth.
evidence: This describes the language acquisition timeline of the delayed signer group.

claim: Early language exposure limitation led to long-lasting effects on various aspects of language processing in delayed deaf signers.
source: Previous research has shown that such early language exposure limitation led to long-lasting effects on various aspects of language processing.
evidence: This statement summarizes findings from previous research.

claim: Delayed deaf signers, even during adulthood with many years of sign language usage, have lower proficiency in phonological, morphological, and syntactic processing of sign language.
source: Behaviorally, these delayed deaf signers, even during adulthood with many years of sign language usage, have lower proficiency in phonological, morphological, and syntactic processing of sign language (Bogliotti et al., 2020; Caselli et al., 2021; Cheng and Mayberry, 2021; Lieberman et al., 2015; Mayberry et al., 2002; Mayberry and Fischer, 1989; Newport, 1990; Tomaszewski et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Brain functional imaging studies have reported decreased activation magnitude in the left inferior frontal and posterior temporal regions in delayed signers during sign sentence judgment tasks.
source: Neurally, brain functional imaging studies have reported decreased activation magnitude in the left inferior frontal and posterior temporal regions in tasks of sign sentence judgments (Mayberry et al., 2011; Richardson et al., 2020; Twomey et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous neuroimaging studies.

claim: Anatomical alterations in language-related regions were reported in signers with delayed L1 acquisition, including reduced cortical volume in the left inferior frontal region, reduced cortical thickness in the left posterior middle temporal region, and reduced fractional anisotropy values in the left arcuate fasciculus.
source: Anatomical alterations in regions typically recruited in language tasks – reduced cortical volume in the left inferior frontal region, reduced cortical thickness in the left posterior middle temporal region, and reduced fractional anisotropy values in the left arcuate fasciculus – were also reported in signers with delayed L1 acquisition (Cheng et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: Studies have reported little effects of delayed L1 acquisition on semantic behaviors, including semantic interference effects, scalar implicature, and accuracy scores of written word semantic tasks.
source: Despite these documented effects of delayed L1 acquisition on phonology, morphology, and syntax (Curtiss, 1977; Lenneberg, 1967; Lillo-Martin and Henner, 2021; Mayberry and Kluender, 2018), studies have reported little effects on semantic behaviors, including semantic interference effects in the picture-sign paradigm (Baus et al., 2008), scalar implicature (Davidson and Mayberry, 2015), or accuracy scores of several written word semantic tasks (e.g. synonym judgment) (Choubsaz and Gheitury, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Similar semantic behaviors may arise from partly different neural representations.
source: However, as shown by the color knowledge in the congenitally blind studies (e.g. Wang et al., 2020), similar semantic behaviors may arise from (partly) different neural representations.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study and represents an inference.

claim: Semantic processing is supported by a multifaceted cognitive system and a complex neural network entailing distributed brain regions.
source: Semantic processing is supported by a multifaceted cognitive system and a complex neural network entailing distributed brain regions (Bi, 2021; Binder and Desai, 2011; Ralph et al., 2017; Martin, 2016), and thus focal neural changes may not necessarily lead to semantic behavioral changes.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: N400 effects in the semantic violation of written sentences were not affected in delayed deaf signers.
source: N400 effects in the semantic violation of written sentences were not affected (Skotara et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous neurophysiological study.

claim: M400 in the picture-sign matching task showed atypical activation patterns in delayed deaf signers, with reduced recruitment of the left fronto-temporal regions and involvement of the right parietal and occipital regions.
source: whereas M400 in the picture-sign matching task showed atypical activation patterns (reduced recruitment of the left fronto-temporal regions and involvement of the right parietal and occipital regions) (Ferjan Ramirez et al., 2016; Ferjan Ramirez et al., 2014; Mayberry et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous neurophysiological studies.

claim: The study recruited 16 native deaf signers and 23 delayed deaf signers.
source: We recruited two adult groups of congenitally or early deaf participants, including 16 native deaf signers and 23 delayed deaf signers (Table 1; Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the participant sample of the study.

claim: Native signers were born in deaf families.
source: Native signers were born in deaf families
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the native signer group.

claim: Delayed signers were born in hearing families and became exposed to Chinese sign language (CSL) between the ages of 4 and 10 (mean ± SD: 6.91±1.62 years of age).
source: delayed signers were born in hearing families and became exposed to Chinese sign language (CSL) between the ages of 4 and 10 (mean ± standard deviation [SD]: 6.91±1.62 years of age).
evidence: This describes the characteristics of the delayed signer group.

claim: Native signers rated their parents to have much more proficient CSL skills than delayed signers did on a 7-point scale (Welch's t31.7 = 13.54, p=1.10 × 10–14).
source: Native signers rated their parents to have much more proficient CSL skills than delayed signers did on a 7-point scale (Welch's t31.7 = 13.54, p=1.10 × 10–14; each participant provided CSL ratings for both parents and the maximum score was used for group comparison).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data.

claim: All deaf participants received formal education in special education programs since elementary school.
source: All deaf participants received formal education in special education programs since elementary school.
evidence: This describes the educational background of the participants.

claim: The two deaf groups were matched on demographic variables (gender, age, years of education, ps > 0.15) and subjective social status during childhood (p = 0.54).
source: The two deaf groups were matched on demographic variables (gender, age, years of education, ps > 0.15) and subjective social status (Adler et al., 2000) during childhood (p = 0.54).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing group matching.

claim: The two groups significantly differed in the education levels of their parents (ps < 0.053), with delayed signers' hearing parents receiving more formal education than the deaf parents of native signers.
source: While the two groups significantly differed in the education levels of their parents (Table 1; ps < 0.053), the direction was in favor of delayed signers as their hearing parents received more formal education than the deaf parents of native signers.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's data.

claim: The two deaf groups were matched on self-reported proficiency of CSL comprehension, production, and lipreading skills (ps > 0.34).
source: In terms of language skills, the two deaf groups were matched on self-reported proficiency of CSL comprehension, production, and lipreading skills (ps > 0.34)
evidence: This is a statistical result showing group matching.

claim: The two deaf groups were matched on the reading disability risk measured by the Adult Reading History Questionnaire (ARHQ) (p = 0.22).
source: and on the reading disability risk measured by the Adult Reading History Questionnaire (ARHQ, Lefly and Pennington, 2000) (p = 0.22).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing group matching.

claim: No significant group differences were found in written word processing evaluated in two reaction-time tasks (visual lexical decision and word-triplet semantic judgment).
source: Written word processing was further evaluated in two reaction-time tasks (i.e. visual lexical decision and word-triplet semantic judgment) and no significant group differences were found (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data, with reference to a figure.

claim: The stimuli of task fMRI were 90 written words that were highly familiar to both groups, including 40 concrete/object words and 50 abstract/nonobject words.
source: The stimuli of task fMRI were 90 written words that were highly familiar to both groups, including 40 concrete/object words varying in sensory and motor properties (animals, face/body parts, artifacts) and 50 abstract/nonobject words varying in social and emotional contents.
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli used in the study.

claim: The 90 words were grouped into 10 categories based on the group-averaged semantic multi-arrangement performances in an independent group of 32 hearing participants.
source: These words were grouped into 10 categories based on the group-averaged semantic multi-arrangement performances in an independent group of 32 hearing participants (see Materials and methods, Figure 1a, and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This describes the categorization method used in the study.

claim: Both deaf groups judged the 90 words to be highly familiar (7-point familiarity ratings from 8 native signers: 6.72±0.17; 13 delayed signers: 6.86±0.15; 7 being most familiar).
source: Both deaf groups judged these words to be highly familiar (7-point familiarity ratings from 8 native signers: 6.72±0.17; 13 delayed signers: 6.86±0.15; 7 being most familiar)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data.

claim: The group-averaged semantic RDMs of the two deaf groups were strongly correlated (Spearman's rho = 0.71, n = 4005).
source: The group-averaged semantic RDMs of the two deaf groups were strongly correlated (Spearman's rho = 0.71, n = 4005; Figure 1a).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data.

claim: At the individual level, correlations with the benchmark (the group-averaged RDM of hearing participants) did not significantly differ between the two deaf groups (Welch's t31.3 = –0.37, p = 0.71).
source: At the individual level, correlations with the benchmark (the group-averaged RDM of hearing participants) did not significantly differ between the two deaf groups (Welch's t31.3 = –0.37, p = 0.71; Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's behavioral data.

claim: The three ROIs (left dATL, pMTG, and IFG) significantly encoded the semantic space in native signers (t15 > 3.04, one-tailed ps < 0.004, Cohen's d > 0.76).
source: As shown in Figure 2, Figure 2—source data 1, the three ROIs significantly encoded the semantic space in native signers (t15 > 3.04, one-tailed ps < 0.004, Cohen's d > 0.76).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data.

claim: In delayed signers, the left dATL and pMTG significantly encoded the semantic space (t22 > 2.07, one-tailed ps < 0.025, Cohen's d > 0.43).
source: In delayed signers, the left dATL and pMTG also significantly encoded the semantic space (t22 > 2.07, one-tailed ps < 0.025, Cohen's d > 0.43)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data.

claim: The left IFG showed a similar, nonsignificant, trend in delayed signers (t22 = 1.31, one-tailed p = 0.10, Cohen's d = 0.27).
source: and the left IFG showed a similar, nonsignificant, trend (t22 = 1.31, one-tailed p = 0.10, Cohen's d = 0.27).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data.

claim: Group differences in semantic encoding were observed in the left dATL (Welch's t36.7 = 3.15, two-tailed p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.98), not in the left pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.26).
source: Critically, group differences were observed in the left dATL (Welch's t36.7 = 3.15, two-tailed p=0.003, Hedges' g = 0.98), not in the left pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.26).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data showing the main finding.

claim: There was no significant group-by-ROI interaction in the two-way ANOVA (F(2,74) = 1.59, p = 0.21).
source: Note that we did not observe a significant group-by-ROI interaction in the two-way ANOVA (F(2,74) = 1.59, p = 0.21).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study's fMRI data.

claim: In native signers, semantic encoding was observed in the left dATL, IFG, pMTG, along with adjacent parietal and occipital areas, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and frontal orbital cortex at the threshold of voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level FWE-corrected p < 0.05.
source: At the threshold of voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level FWE-corrected p < 0.05, in native signers, the semantic encoding was observed in the left dATL, IFG, pMTG, along with adjacent parietal and occipital areas, dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and frontal orbital cortex.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain searchlight RSA analysis.

claim: In delayed signers, no brain regions survived the whole-brain correction at the threshold of voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level FWE-corrected p < 0.05.
source: In delayed signers, no brain regions survived the whole-brain correction
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain searchlight RSA analysis.

claim: At a more lenient threshold of voxel p < 0.001, cluster size >10 voxels, semantic encoding could be observed in the left dATL, IFG, and clusters scattered in the left inferior parietal and occipital regions in delayed signers.
source: at a more lenient threshold of voxel p < 0.001, cluster size >10 voxels, semantic encoding could be observed in the left dATL, IFG, and clusters scattered in the left inferior parietal and occipital regions.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain searchlight RSA analysis at a lenient threshold.

claim: The whole-brain contrast between the two deaf groups peaked at the left dATL at the threshold of voxel p < 0.001, which was also the largest cluster (peak MNI coordinates: –60, 6,–20, peak t = 5.87, 162 voxels).
source: The whole-brain contrast between the two deaf groups peaked at the left dATL at the threshold of voxel p < 0.001, which was also the largest cluster (peak MNI coordinates: –60, 6,–20, peak t = 5.87, 162 voxels), converging well with the ROI results in that native signers showed stronger semantic encoding than delayed signers in the left dATL ROI.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain group comparison analysis.

claim: The largest cluster in the whole-brain contrast was not large enough to survive the whole-brain correction (cluster FWE-corrected p = 0.22), but the top 10 voxels survived the voxel-level correction of FWE-corrected p < 0.05.
source: While this cluster was not large enough to survive the whole-brain correction (cluster FWE-corrected p = 0.22), the top 10 voxels survived the voxel-level correction of FWE-corrected p < 0.05.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the whole-brain analysis.

claim: No areas were found to show significantly increased semantic information in delayed signers compared with native signers at the conventional threshold.
source: No areas were found to show significantly increased semantic information in delayed signers compared with native signers at the conventional threshold.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain group comparison analysis.

claim: The two deaf groups showed comparable similarities to the hearing benchmark when using continuous behavioral measures (Welch's t23.0 = –0.12, two-tailed p = 0.90).
source: The two deaf groups showed comparable similarities to the hearing benchmark (by correlating each deaf subject's RDM with the group-averaged RDM of hearing subjects, Welch's t23.0 = –0.12, two-tailed p = 0.90).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis using continuous semantic measures.

claim: Significant group differences in left dATL semantic encoding were observed for both the categorical RDM (Welch's t31.0 = 3.06, two-tailed p = 0.005, Hedges' g = 0.98) and the continuous behavioral semantic RDM (Welch's t37.0 = 2.47, two-tailed p = 0.018, Hedges' g = 0.76).
source: Significant group differences were observed (Figure 3; Figure 3—source data 1), for both the categorical RDM (Welch's t31.0 = 3.06, two-tailed p = 0.005, Hedges' g = 0.98) and the continuous behavioral semantic RDM (Welch's t37.0 = 2.47, two-tailed p = 0.018, Hedges' g = 0.76)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis.

claim: Significant semantic encoding in the dATL was observed in both analyses for native signers (one-tailed ps < 0.003) and neither for delayed signers (one-tailed ps > 0.42).
source: with significant semantic encoding in the dATL observed in both analyses for native signers (one-tailed ps < 0.003) and neither for delayed signers (one-tailed ps > 0.42).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis.

claim: Significant group differences in semantic encoding were observed in the ATL using a commonly used language mask (Welch's t33.1 = 3.71, two-tailed p = 7.53 × 10–4, Hedges' g = 1.18), which also survived the Bonferroni correction.
source: As shown in Figure 4, Figure 4—source data 1, again we observed significant group differences in the ATL (Welch's t33.1 = 3.71, two-tailed p = 7.53 × 10–4, Hedges' g = 1.18), which also survived the Bonferroni correction.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis using an alternative ROI definition.

claim: Other language-sensitive regions did not reach significance in group differences, with the tendency for the same direction of semantic encoding reduction (ps > 0.065, uncorrected).
source: Other language-sensitive regions did not reach significance, with the tendency for the same direction of semantic encoding reduction (ps > 0.065, uncorrected).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis.

claim: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant main effect of group (F(1, 37) = 6.80, p=0.013) and no significant ROI-by-group interaction (F(5, 185) = 0.823, p=0.535) in the language-sensitive regions analysis.
source: Two-way ANOVA showed a significant main effect of group (F(1, 37) = 6.80, p=0.013) and no significant ROI-by-group interaction (F(5, 185) = 0.823, p=0.535), indicating that delayed L1 acquisition resulted in widespread reduced semantic representations in the language regions, with the effects in the ATL consistently robust.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the validation analysis.

claim: Delayed L1 acquisition resulted in widespread reduced semantic representations in the language regions, with the effects in the ATL consistently robust.
source: indicating that delayed L1 acquisition resulted in widespread reduced semantic representations in the language regions, with the effects in the ATL consistently robust.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: All three ROIs (the left dATL, IFG, and pMTG) exhibited significant abstractness preference in both deaf groups (native group: paired ts > 3.72, df = 15, one-tailed ps <0.001, Cohen's ds > 0.93; delayed group: paired ts > 2.13, df = 22, one-tailed ps < 0.02, Cohen's ds>0.44).
source: At the ROI level (Figure 5—source data 1), all three ROIs (the left dATL, IFG, and pMTG) exhibited significant abstractness preference in both deaf groups (Figure 5a; native group: paired ts > 3.72, df = 15, one-tailed ps <0.001, Cohen's ds > 0.93; delayed group: paired ts > 2.13, df = 22, one-tailed ps < 0.02, Cohen's ds>0.44)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the univariate analysis.

claim: The group × word type interaction reached statistical significance only in the left dATL (F(1,37) = 4.91, p = 0.033), not in the left pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.30).
source: The group × word type interaction reached statistical significance only in the left dATL (F(1,37) = 4.91, p = 0.033), not in the left pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.30).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the univariate analysis showing the main finding.

claim: In the left dATL, native signers exhibited greater semantic abstractness effects than delayed signers.
source: In the left dATL native signers exhibited greater semantic abstractness effects than delayed signers.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical results.

claim: The main effects of group were not significant in any of the three ROIs (ps > 0.057).
source: The main effects of group were not significant in any of the three ROIs (ps > 0.057).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the univariate analysis.

claim: There were no significant group-by-ROI interaction in the semantic abstractness effects (F(2,74) = 0.50, p = 0.61).
source: There were no significant group-by-ROI interaction (F(2,74) = 0.50, p = 0.61).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the univariate analysis.

claim: Using individualized functional ROI (fROI) analysis, the group × word type interaction was again observed in the left dATL (F(1,37) = 6.20, p = 0.017), not in the pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.58).
source: As shown in Figure 5b, the group × word type interaction was again observed in the left dATL (F(1,37) = 6.20, p = 0.017), not in the pMTG or IFG (ps > 0.58).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the individualized fROI validation analysis.

claim: Main effects of group were not found in the individualized fROI analysis (ps > 0.18).
source: Main effects of group were not found (ps > 0.18).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the individualized fROI validation analysis.

claim: For native signers, semantic abstractness reached significance in the left dATL at the threshold of voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level FWE-corrected p < 0.05 (peak MNI coordinates: –58, 4,–8, peak t = 7.27, 209 voxels).
source: For native signers, at the threshold of voxel-level p < 0.001, cluster-level FWE-corrected p < 0.05, semantic abstractness reached significance in the left dATL (peak MNI coordinates: –58, 4,–8, peak t = 7.27, 209 voxels).
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain univariate analysis.

claim: For delayed signers, no regions survived the whole-brain threshold for semantic abstractness; at a lenient threshold of voxel p < 0.001, cluster size >10 voxels, abstractness could be observed in the left pMTG and dATL.
source: For delayed signers, no regions survived the whole-brain threshold; at a lenient threshold of voxel p < 0.001, cluster size >10 voxels, abstractness could be observed in the left pMTG and dATL, which are consistent with the ROI results above.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain univariate analysis.

claim: The whole-brain between-group comparisons of the semantic abstractness effects did not yield any areas surviving the conventional whole-brain correction threshold.
source: The whole-brain between-group comparisons of the semantic abstractness effects did not yield any areas surviving the conventional whole-brain correction threshold.
evidence: This is a result from the whole-brain group comparison analysis.

claim: Delayed signers reported significantly lower writing ability (Welch's t31.0 = –2.91, p = 0.007, Hedges' g = –0.93) and a tendency of lower reading speeds (Welch's t26.2 = –1.89, p = 0.07, Hedges' g = –0.62) in the ARHQ than native signers.
source: However, delayed signers did report significantly lower writing ability (Welch's t31.0 = –2.91, p = 0.007, Hedges' g = –0.93) and a tendency of lower reading speeds (Welch's t26.2 = –1.89, p = 0.07, Hedges' g = –0.62) in the ARHQ than native signers (Table 1).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the background questionnaire data.

claim: For both the multivariate RSA and univariate abstractness effects, the direct effects of group remained largely significant (ps < 0.074), whereas the mediation effects did not approach statistical significance (ps > 0.52) in mediation analyses examining whether writing or reading speed mediated the group differences in neural semantic effects in the left dATL.
source: For both the multivariate RSA and univariate abstractness effects, the direct effects of group remained largely significant (ps < 0.074), whereas the mediation effects did not approach statistical significance (ps > 0.52), based on 5000 times bootstrapping resampling.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the mediation analysis.

claim: The reduced dATL semantic effects induced by delayed L1 acquisition were not fully attributable to written language processes.
source: That is, the reduced dATL semantic effects induced by delayed L1 acquisition were not fully attributable to written language processes.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mediation analysis results.

claim: Early-life language acquisition is necessary for the left dATL to exhibit the typical semantic organization in adulthood.
source: That is, early-life language acquisition – critical to language system neurodevelopment – is necessary for the left dATL to exhibit the typical semantic organization in adulthood.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The results provide the first positive evidence for the effect of language experience on driving the semantic functional development of a particular brain region.
source: These results provide the first positive evidence for the effect of language experience on driving the semantic functional development of a particular brain region.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and significance of the findings.

claim: The group effect is not specific to the dATL relative to other brain regions, as there was no significant group-by-ROI interaction in either the RSA or the univariate analyses.
source: First, is this group effect specific to the dATL, relative to other brain regions? We do not have evidence for such a strong region specificity. We did not observe a significant group-by-ROI interaction in either the RSA or the univariate analyses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results.

claim: The dATL is not claimed to be the only region that derives semantic representation from language experience.
source: We are thus not claiming that the dATL is the only region that derives semantic representation from language experience, but choose to focus the following discussion on this region because of the robust positive effects here.
evidence: This clarifies the scope of the claims being made.

claim: The manipulation of the current study varies on language exposure while matching on sensory experiences.
source: The manipulation of the current study – the two groups of deaf signers – varies on the language exposure while matching on the sensory experiences (see below), and thus did not test the presence or absence of sensory-derived semantic representations.
evidence: This describes the experimental design and its implications.

claim: Evidence from congenitally blind studies does not support additional sensory-derived semantic encoding in the dATL.
source: That is, evidence from congenitally blind studies does not support the additional sensory-derived semantic encoding here.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from previous literature.

claim: It is parsimonious to propose that the dATL's contribution to semantic encoding is specific to language, and not sensory-derived representations.
source: While drawing negative conclusions is always difficult, we reason that it is parsimonious, based on available data, to propose that the dATL's contribution to semantic encoding is specific to language, and not sensory-derived representations.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the current and previous findings.

claim: The two deaf groups were matched on sensory experiences (both similarly profoundly deaf), a wide range of nonlinguistic environmental variables including socioeconomic status (except for parents' education backgrounds, which were better for the delayed signer group), the length and level of formal education, through which largely comparable sign language and word reading skills were achieved.
source: The two deaf groups were matched on sensory experiences (both similarly profoundly deaf), a wide range of nonlinguistic environmental variables including the socioeconomic status (except for parents' education backgrounds, which were better for the delayed signer group), the length and level of formal education, through which largely comparable sign language and word reading skills were achieved.
evidence: This summarizes the matching of the two groups on various factors.

claim: The salient difference between the two groups was the early-life language experience (before 6.9 years of age – the mean age of acquisition in the delayed signer group).
source: The salient difference was the early-life language experience (before 6.9 years of age – the mean age of acquisition in our delayed signer group).
evidence: This identifies the key variable that differs between the two groups.

claim: Deaf children with limited access to natural language often spontaneously develop homesign systems, which share some aspects with natural language.
source: Notably, deaf children with limited access to natural language often spontaneously develop homesign systems, which share some aspects with natural language (Goldin-Meadow, 2003).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Deaf children could use homesigns to produce generic utterances in a similar manner to typically developed children.
source: For instance, they could use homesigns to produce generic utterances in a similar manner to typically developed children (Goldin-Meadow et al., 2005).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Early homesign/aid measures and later formal education for sign and written language experiences are insufficient for typical dATL neurodevelopment.
source: Critically, our positive results of the robust group differences in the dATL suggest that early homesign/aid measures and later formal education for sign and written language experiences are insufficient for typical dATL neurodevelopment
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: Full-fledged language experience during early infancy and childhood (before school age) plays a necessary role in typical dATL neurodevelopment.
source: the full-fledged language experience during early infancy and childhood (before school age) plays a necessary role in this process.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results.

claim: A lack of early language exposure may lead to alterations beyond the language system, affecting non-language cognitive domains such as working memory or theory of mind in children.
source: A further variable to consider is that a lack of early language exposure may lead to alterations beyond the language system, affecting non-language cognitive domains such as working memory or theory of mind in children (Marshall et al., 2015; Richardson et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The positive evidence of working memory or theory of mind variables in dATL functionality is lacking.
source: While we cannot rule out the effects of these potential intermediate cognitive processes, the positive evidence of these variables in dATL functionality is lacking.
evidence: This is an assessment of the available evidence.

claim: The most direct manipulation and parsimonious account for the dATL effects is language-related.
source: The most direct manipulation and parsimonious account for the dATL effects is language-related.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental design and results.

claim: The dATL shows a functional preference for abstract words, which are less salient in sensory attributes than concrete words and are assumed to entail more language processes such as context diversity.
source: It shows a functional preference for abstract words, which are less salient in sensory attributes than concrete words and are assumed to entail more language processes such as context diversity (e.g. Binder et al., 2009; Bucur and Papagno, 2021; Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In congenitally blind individuals, the dATL encodes visual knowledge such as color and the activity strength is negatively modulated by perceptibility.
source: In congenitally blind individuals, it encodes visual knowledge such as color and the activity strength is negatively modulated by perceptibility (Bottini et al., 2020; Striem-Amit et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dATL is sensitive to semantic composition, such as in two-word phrases or sentences.
source: It is sensitive to semantic composition, such as in two-word phrases or sentences (Pallier et al., 2011; Pylkkänen, 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The dATL is functionally and structurally connected with other language-sensitive regions.
source: This region is functionally and structurally connected with other language-sensitive regions (Fan et al., 2014; Friederici et al., 2017; Ralph et al., 2017; Pascual et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The early-life resting-state functional connectivity patterns of the left temporal pole significantly predict performances in tasks entailing semantic processes, not in tasks of phonological skills or rapid automatized naming, at about 6.5 years of age.
source: Finally, a recent neurodevelopmental study shows that the early-life resting-state functional connectivity patterns of the left temporal pole significantly predict performances in tasks entailing semantic processes, not in tasks of phonological skills or rapid automatized naming, at about 6.5 years of age (Yu et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: The parsimonious proposal accounting for the findings together would be that the dATL represents knowledge derived from language (e.g., from higher-order word relations).
source: Together with the positive evidence of early language experience in developing typical semantic representation in the dATL reported here, the parsimonious proposal accounting for them together would be that the dATL represents knowledge derived from language (e.g. from higher-order word relations).
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation based on the current and previous findings.

claim: Without early language exposure, the semantic structure representation and the abstractness preference in the dATL are reduced.
source: Without early language exposure, the semantic structure representation and the abstractness preference here are reduced.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental results.

claim: The findings extend beyond the majority of the neurocognitive semantic theories, which mainly focus on the representing, binding, and controlling of knowledge derived from nonlinguistic multisensory experiences.
source: Together, this package of findings extends beyond the majority of the neurocognitive semantic theories, which mainly focus on the representing, binding, and controlling of knowledge derived from nonlinguistic multisensory experiences (Binder, 2016; Ralph et al., 2017; Martin, 2016; but see Mahon and Caramazza, 2008).
evidence: This statement compares the findings to existing theories, supported by citations.

claim: The recently developed dual-neural-coding framework for semantic knowledge explicitly proposes that the human brain has developed regions (the dATL) for language-derived semantic representations, in addition to the sensory-derived knowledge representations.
source: The recently developed dual-neural-coding framework for semantic knowledge (Bi, 2021), which explicitly proposes that the human brain has developed regions (the dATL) for language-derived semantic representations, in addition to the sensory-derived knowledge representations, naturally accommodates these observations.
evidence: This statement describes a theoretical framework supported by citation.

claim: Language, as a symbolic system, allows us to convey and manipulate meanings free from sensorimotor experiences and plays a key role in knowledge transmission and accumulation across individuals and generations.
source: Language, as a symbolic system, allows us to convey and manipulate meanings free from sensorimotor experiences and plays a key role in knowledge transmission and accumulation across individuals and generations (Gelman and Roberts, 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to previous research.

claim: The existence of the language-derived knowledge neural system may lay the foundation for the efficient storage and manipulation of semantic knowledge, particularly abstract knowledge without tangible and consistent sensorimotor referents.
source: The existence of the language-derived knowledge neural system may lay the foundation for the efficient storage and manipulation of semantic knowledge, particularly abstract knowledge without tangible and consistent sensorimotor referents (Bi, 2021).
evidence: This is a theoretical proposal supported by citation.

claim: Previous studies have reported that delayed L1 acquisition associates with reduced cortical volume in the left inferior frontal region, reduced cortical thickness in the left posterior middle temporal region, and reduced fractional anisotropy values in the left arcuate fasciculus, and not ATL or its related white matter tracts.
source: Previous studies have reported that delayed L1 acquisition associates with reduced cortical volume in the left inferior frontal region, reduced cortical thickness in the left posterior middle temporal region, and the reduced fractional anisotropy values in the left arcuate fasciculus that structurally connects the two regions, and not ATL or its related white matter tracts (Cheng et al., 2023; Cheng et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous anatomical studies.

claim: The findings of semantic functional alterations in the dATL are not easily attributable to broad anatomical changes associated with late L1 acquisition.
source: Our findings of semantic functional alterations in the dATL are thus not easily attributable to broad anatomical changes associated with late L1 acquisition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn by comparing the current findings with previous anatomical studies.

claim: For phonological and syntactic processes, both visible behavioral underdevelopment and brain functional changes were observed in delayed deaf signers.
source: Notably, different from phonological and syntactic processes, where both visible behavioral underdevelopment (e.g. Caselli et al., 2021; Cheng and Mayberry, 2021; Mayberry et al., 2002) and brain functional changes (Mayberry et al., 2011; Richardson et al., 2020; Twomey et al., 2020) were observed
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: For semantics, only brain functional changes in the dATL were observed but no visible behavioral effects.
source: for semantics we only observed brain functional changes in the dATL but no visible behavioral effects.
evidence: This summarizes the findings of the current study.

claim: Deaf delayed signers did not show differences to controls in semantic interference effects in the picture-sign paradigm, scalar implicature, or N400 measures.
source: Consistent with the literature where deaf delayed signers did not show differences to controls in semantic interference effects in the picture-sign paradigm (Baus et al., 2008), scalar implicature (Davidson and Mayberry, 2015), or N400 measures (Skotara et al., 2012)
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The study did not observe visible differences in terms of semantic distance structures or reaction time of lexical decision and word-triplet semantic judgment between the two deaf groups.
source: we did not observe visible differences in terms of semantic distance structures (Figure 1a) or reaction time of lexical decision and word-triplet semantic judgment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This summarizes the behavioral findings of the current study.

claim: The seeming neuro-behavior discrepancy might be related to the multifaceted, distributed nature of the cognitive and neural basis of semantics more broadly.
source: As reasoned in the Introduction, this seeming neuro-behavior discrepancy might be related to the multifaceted, distributed nature of the cognitive and neural basis of semantics more broadly.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the discrepancy between neural and behavioral findings.

claim: The general semantic behavioral tasks employed could be achieved with representations derived from multiple types of experiences, supported by highly distributed neural systems, including those not affected by delayed L1 acquisition in regions beyond the dATL.
source: The general semantic behavioral tasks we employed could be achieved with representations derived from multiple types of experiences, supported by highly distributed neural systems (e.g. Bi, 2021; Binder and Desai, 2011; Ralph et al., 2017; Martin, 2016), including those not affected by delayed L1 acquisition in regions beyond the dATL.
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By manipulation of early language experience by nature, the study was able to positively identify a human brain region – dATL – robustly supporting word meanings derived from language experience, in contrast to those grounding nonlinguistic, sensory experiences.
source: To conclude, by manipulation of early language experience by nature we were able to positively identify a human brain region – dATL – robustly supporting word meanings derived from language experience, in contrast to those grounding nonlinguistic, sensory experiences.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings highlight the role of language in forming specific neural semantic representations in the human brain.
source: These findings highlight the role of language in forming specific neural semantic representations in the human brain, and raise new questions about the ontogenetic mechanisms of this intriguing neural structure.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the significance of the findings.

claim: Thirty-nine congenitally or early deaf adults and 33 hearing college students were recruited for the fMRI study.
source: Thirty-nine congenitally or early deaf adults and 33 hearing college students (15 males, mean age 21.97 ± 2.58 years, range: 18–28 years, all native Mandarin Chinese speakers) were recruited for the fMRI study.
evidence: This describes the participant sample.

claim: All deaf participants reported being severely or profoundly deaf from birth, except for one native signer and three delayed signers who reported becoming deaf before the age of 2 due to medication side effects.
source: For hearing loss conditions, all deaf participants reported being severely or profoundly deaf from birth, except for one native signer and three delayed signers who reported becoming deaf before the age of 2 due to medication side effects.
evidence: This describes the hearing status of the participants.

claim: Hearing thresholds in decibels (dB) were available in 23 deaf participants (native: 11/16; delayed: 12/23) and confirmed severe to profound hearing loss (range: 85–120 dB).
source: Hearing thresholds in decibels (dB) were available in 23 deaf participants (native: 11/16; delayed: 12/23) and confirmed severe to profound hearing loss (range: 85–120 dB).
evidence: This provides objective hearing loss data for a subset of participants.

claim: Speech comprehension was reported to be very poor in deaf participants, even with the use of hearing aids.
source: Speech comprehension was reported to be very poor, even with the use of hearing aids.
evidence: This describes the speech comprehension abilities of the participants.

claim: All participants were right-handed, except for three native signers (one was ambidextrous and two were left-handed).
source: All participants were right-handed, except for three native signers (one was ambidextrous and two were left-handed) (measured by the Edinburgh inventory, Oldfield, 1971).
evidence: This describes the handedness of the participants.

claim: The study was approved by the Human Subject Review Committee at Peking University (2017-09-01), China, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
source: The study was approved by the Human Subject Review Committee at Peking University (2017-09-01), China, in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.
evidence: This provides ethical approval information.

claim: Concrete/object words varied in sensory and motor attributes and included 10 animals, 10 face or body parts, 10 tools, and 10 common large household objects.
source: Concrete/object words varied in sensory and motor attributes and included 10 animals (e.g. panda), 10 face or body parts (e.g. shoulder), 10 tools (e.g. hammer), and 10 common large household objects (e.g. microwave).
evidence: This describes the composition of the concrete word stimuli.

claim: Abstract/nonobject words varied in social and emotional associations.
source: Abstract/nonobject words varied in social and emotional associations (e.g. cause, violence).
evidence: This describes the composition of the abstract word stimuli.

claim: All words were disyllabic except for five object words ('cat' and 'bed' are monosyllabic and 'giraffe', 'microwave', and 'washing machine' are trisyllabic in Chinese).
source: All words were disyllabic except for five object words ('cat' and 'bed' are monosyllabic and 'giraffe', 'microwave', and 'washing machine' are trisyllabic in Chinese).
evidence: This describes the syllabic structure of the word stimuli.

claim: All words were primarily used as nouns except for 10 words denoting emotional states (nine were primarily used as adjectives and one as a verb).
source: All words were primarily used as nouns except for 10 words denoting emotional states (nine were primarily used as adjectives and one as a verb).
evidence: This describes the grammatical categories of the word stimuli.

claim: The concrete and abstract words were matched on the number of strokes (17.23 ± 5.80 vs 16.14 ± 3.98; t88 = 1.05, p = 0.30).
source: The concrete and abstract words were matched on the number of strokes (a measure of visual complexity for Chinese words; 17.23 ± 5.80 vs 16.14 ± 3.98; t88 = 1.05, p = 0.30).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing stimulus matching.

claim: Concrete/object words were less frequent in a Mandarin Chinese corpus than abstract/nonobject words (log word frequency: 1.05±0.73 vs 1.62 ± 0.68; t88 = –3.83, p < 0.001).
source: While concrete/object words were less frequent in a Mandarin Chinese corpus (Sun et al., 1997) than abstract/nonobject words (log word frequency: 1.05±0.73 vs 1.62 ± 0.68; t88 = –3.83, p < 0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical result describing stimulus properties.

claim: Concrete/object words were rated as more subjectively familiar than abstract/nonobject words in either hearing (6.79 ± 0.16 vs 6.22 ± 0.26; t88 = 12.05, p < 0.001) or deaf (6.85 ± 0.07 vs 6.77 ± 0.13; t88 = 3.41, p < 0.001) participants.
source: the former were rated as more subjectively familiar than the latter in either hearing (6.79 ± 0.16 vs 6.22 ± 0.26; t88 = 12.05, p < 0.001) or deaf (6.85 ± 0.07 vs 6.77 ± 0.13; t88 = 3.41, p < 0.001) participants.
evidence: This is a statistical result describing stimulus properties.

claim: Participants performed the semantic distance judgment task attentively, with overall miss rates lower than 22.1% (median: 1.4%).
source: Participants performed this task attentively, with overall miss rates lower than 22.1% (median: 1.4%).
evidence: This is a behavioral result showing task performance.

claim: All participants had head motion less than 1.97 mm/1.95°, except for one hearing participant showing excessive head motion in 2 runs (>2 mm/2°).
source: All participants had head motion less than 1.97 mm/1.95°, except for one hearing participant showing excessive head motion in 2 runs (>2 mm/2°); we thus analyzed the remaining 8 runs of fMRI data for this participant.
evidence: This describes the quality control for head motion in the fMRI data.

claim: The two deaf groups exhibited comparable framewise displacement (FD) during scanning (native: 0.12±0.04; delayed: 0.11±0.04; Welch's t29.1 = 0.77, p = 0.45).
source: We also estimated each participant's framewise displacement (FD) from translations and rotations (Power et al., 2012); the two deaf groups exhibited comparable FD during scanning (native: 0.12±0.04; delayed: 0.11±0.04; Welch's t29.1 = 0.77, p = 0.45).
evidence: This is a statistical result showing group matching on head motion.
